growth_story.headline: Reforms from the mid-1990s ended a long slump; income per person has grown every year but one since 1999, though fast population growth keeps the gains modest.
growth_story.arc: Socialist policies and economic isolation ended in collapse in the 1980s. Reforms began in 1986 but moved slowly: from 1990 to 1998 income per person grew 0.4 percent a year, and it fell every year from 1991 to 1994. In the mid-1990s the reforms began to pay off. A single exchange rate, freer imports, a rebuilt banking system, lower inflation and debt relief drew in private and foreign investment, and from 1999 to 2025 income per person grew 2.9 percent a year, with the best years in the early 2000s and a high of 4.7 percent in 2011. Since 2010 growth has relied more on public infrastructure spending while private and foreign investment fell, and the pace slowed from 3.3 percent a year in 2006–2015 to 2.1 percent in 2016–2025, including a fall of 1.0 percent in 2020. Income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025, but fast population growth means strong growth in the economy as a whole turns into much smaller gains per person.

threads.title: Socialism, collapse and slow reform
threads.text: State control, socialist self-reliance and isolation led to economic collapse in the 1980s. Prices, the exchange rate and trade were freed step by step from 1986, but growth stayed weak, and income per person grew only 0.4 percent a year from 1990 to 1998.

citations.title: Tanzania: The Story of an African Transition

threads.title: Mid-1990s reforms take hold
threads.text: From the mid-1990s a unified exchange rate, freer imports, a restructured banking system and tighter public finances brought inflation down and drew in private and foreign investment. Debt relief removed almost all foreign debt, and income per person has grown every year since 1999 except 2020.

citations.title: Tanzania: The Story of an African Transition
citations.quote: It was only in the mid-1990s that the reforms really began to pay off.

citations.title: Tanzania: The Story of an African Transition

threads.title: Public investment takes the lead
threads.text: Since 2010 public infrastructure spending has become the main source of new capital, while private investment and foreign investment fell. Growth in income per person slowed from 3.3 percent a year in 2006–2015 to 2.1 percent in 2016–2025.

threads.title: Fast population, few formal jobs
threads.text: The population grows fast and formal jobs have not kept pace, so many people rely on informal work. The World Bank finds poverty has fallen only slowly because growth is concentrated in sectors that use a lot of capital and have weak links to the livelihoods of the poorest.

threads.title: A reform turn since 2021
threads.text: President Samia Suluhu Hassan took office in March 2021 after President Magufuli's death and has backed reforms that give private firms a bigger role. The IMF ties its outlook to mining, agriculture and tourism and warns that reform delays could weaken growth.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 2.9 percent in 2025, the fastest since 2017, helped by services and by higher government spending before the October 2025 elections. In the first half of 2026 an oil price spike tied to conflict in the Middle East raised fuel costs and put pressure on the balance of payments, while gold exports and tourism softened the blow. In July 2026 the IMF completed the final reviews of its Extended Credit Facility loan.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe strong, steady growth and expect it to speed up. The data on income per person tell a quieter story: growth per person slowed from 3.3 percent a year in 2006–2015 to 2.1 percent in 2016–2025, because the population grows fast, and the World Bank notes that poverty has fallen only slowly.
